New regulations released this month, will allow the Ministry of Education to outsource the management, operation, development and financing of public schools, educational services and government education assets to private-sector, foreign-investor and non-profit partners for the first time.

author: Hamzah Wilson
headline: Founder & CEO at Ardeenah | I connect investors with land, developers and construction partners in Saudi Arabia, especially Makkah & Madinah
text:
Non-oil revenues now cover 37% of Saudi government spending. That compares to 16% in previous years.

This is what fiscal transformation looks like in practice.

The Kingdom is building capacity to operate at scale without depending on hydrocarbon revenue to fund day-to-day operations.

Three implications:

• Public-sector projects can proceed through oil-price volatility without halting capital deployment. Resilience in the budget translates to resilience in contracts.

• Private-sector partners face a more stable counterparty. When government spending is less exposed to oil swings, procurement and development timelines hold.

• Vision 2030 targets become more credible. A government that can fund 37% of operations off non-oil sources in 2026 can plausibly reach broader diversification by 2030.

The numbers show what policy documents promise.

Worth noting if you are looking at Saudi counterparty risk or long-cycle deployment.

via Saudi Gazette

#SaudiArabia #Vision2030 #CapitalMarkets

author: Ion S.
headline: Founder, Rebium | Programmable settlement with a built-in 1% rebate
text:
From day one, the ambition behind Rebium has been clear: help Saudi Arabia strengthen domestic capital formation and support the long-term delivery of Vision 2030.
The core design is simple. 75% of the transaction allocation is directed into an institutional investment structure intended to be linked to the PIF. That capital is reinvested. The returns generated from those investments are what fund the rebate mechanism itself.
In this model, settlement activity does not just move value — it builds a permanent capital base inside the system. The more the system is used, the stronger the internal funding capacity becomes.
Saudi Arabia remains the natural home for this architecture. If the right partnership does not materialise within the Saudi fintech ecosystem, the work will continue elsewhere.
The goal is not only to finance projects. It is to create a self-reinforcing mechanism that helps sustain them.

In broader terms:

Everton effectively became a cautionary tale of how stadium costs can contribute to financial strain, with Farhad Moshiri repeatedly funding the club before eventually selling his stake and TFG had to finish off with the Stadium funding.

Manchester United sold a minority stake to INEOS, bringing in fresh capital, yet still announced ambitious stadium plans without a fully detailed funding solution being publicly in place at the time.

So your underlying point is that PIF may be looking at what happened elsewhere and thinking: why carry the entire burden ourselves when external investment can help fund a stadium project?

That doesn't necessarily point to an owner wanting out. If anything, it can be viewed as a more commercially disciplined approach to funding a major infrastructure project.

Shariah-screened indices have existed for public equities since 1999. For private tech, nothing comparable followed for more than 2 decades.

With global Islamic finance assets now exceeding $6.5 trillion according to the 2026 Islamic Finance Development Report, Stableton and Mnaara partnered to close that gap with the Mnaara Unicorn Top 15 Semi-Liquid Strategy:
→ A rule selects the 15 most valuable private tech companies in developed markets, equally weighted
→ Every company is screened against Shariah standards
→ The screening is overseen independently

An index made Shariah screening practical for public equities more than 25 years ago. We see the same approach now reaching private technology companies.

headline: Ex-KPMG | ACA | Fractional CFO | Financial Modeling, Valuation and Transaction Support for Advisory Firms | Supported USD 250M+ in Debt and
text:
REAL EVENT

A business valuation can change without the business itself changing.

Recently, our advisory team was engaged to value a manufacturing business in the GCC that produced wooden pallets used in goods transportation.

We completed the valuation at approximately OMR 2.7 million (around USD 7 million) and began assisting the owners with the sale process.

At the time, buyer interest was relatively limited.

Then, something changed.

A new regulatory requirement in the GCC market made palletization mandatory for applicable imported goods. This created a potentially significant increase in demand for the industry's products.

The result?

We started seeing greater interest from potential buyers, while the business's growth prospects began to look different.

The interesting part was that the manufacturing facility, historical financial statements, and existing operations had not suddenly transformed.

What had changed was the external environment and the potential future earning capacity of the business.

This experience reinforced three important lessons for me:

1. Valuation is forward-looking. 

Historical EBITDA matters, but future demand, regulatory developments, industry dynamics, and competitive positioning can materially influence what a buyer is willing to pay.

2. An opportunity is not the same as value creation.

text:
Most corporate finance profiles in the GCC read like transaction tombstones. They list deal sizes, but fail to show execution ownership.

Recruiters give a profile eight seconds. If they only see passive deal involvement, they move on. Middle East dealmaking is consolidating into platform-level scale: 91% of 2026 YTD transaction value sits in scaled M&A and debt, averaging $718 million per transaction.

Working on Americold Realty Trust's c.$834m IPO showed me what that scale requires. Coordinating with the US teams for drafting and due diligence of an S-1 filing proved that deals close on regulatory rigor, not financial modeling alone.

If your profile frames you as back-office support rather than an execution partner, you miss the mark for Gulf platforms.

Dealmakers are never hired for spreadsheet speed; they are hired for underwriting conviction under regulatory scrutiny.

Are GCC investment teams filtering out top execution talent by prioritising brand logos over direct transaction ownership?

headline: Aspiring CPO | Head of IT Procurement | 28 Yrs Driving $1B+ Tech Spend Across BFSI, Telecom & GCCs | Cloud, SaaS & Managed Services Sourcing
text:
A GCC’s first purchase order and its hundredth look very different. The way procurement works in between is what decides whether the centre grows well or grows messy.

The Zinnov-Nasscom India GCC Landscape 2026 sorts India’s GCCs into four stages:

▪️ Outpost: 13%

▪️ Satellite: 43%

▪️ Portfolio Hub: 39%

▪️ Transformation Hub: 5%

So about 56% sit in the first two stages, and only 5% have reached the most advanced one. The report also counts 583 mid-market GCCs and 504 PE-backed GCCs, which means many centres are new, growing, and building their processes as they go.

That is a big opportunity for procurement professionals. Here is how I think about it, stage by stage:

Outpost and Satellite. The centre mostly uses the parent’s contracts and systems. 

Procurement’s job is to keep it simple and compliant, and to avoid duplicate buying.

Portfolio Hub. The centre owns more work and starts buying for itself. This is where local supplier panels, delegated authority and clear approval rules start to matter.

Transformation Hub. The centre drives innovation for the group. Procurement becomes a partner in choosing technology and partners, not just a processor of orders.

The common mistake is building Stage 3 processes too early, or running Stage 1 processes for too long. Both cost money.

After 28 years across Banking, Telecom, and Technology, I have seen that procurement works best when it grows with the business it supports, one step ahead and not three steps behind.

text:
Most corporate finance profiles in the GCC read like transaction tombstones. They list deal sizes, but fail to show execution ownership.

Recruiters give a profile eight seconds. If they only see passive deal involvement, they move on. Middle East dealmaking is consolidating into platform-level scale: 91% of 2026 YTD transaction value sits in scaled M&A and debt, averaging $718 million per transaction.

Working on Americold Realty Trust's c.$834m IPO showed me what that scale requires. Coordinating with the US teams for drafting and due diligence of an S-1 filing proved that deals close on regulatory rigor, not financial modeling alone.

If your profile frames you as back-office support rather than an execution partner, you miss the mark for Gulf platforms.

Dealmakers are never hired for spreadsheet speed; they are hired for underwriting conviction under regulatory scrutiny.

Are GCC investment teams filtering out top execution talent by prioritising brand logos over direct transaction ownership?

A major offshore engineering development has emerged in Saudi Arabia.

On November 25, Italian engineering company Saipem announced two new offshore contracts worth approximately $650 million under its long-term agreement with Saudi Aramco.

The projects cover offshore fields including Abu Safah, Safaniya, Manifa, Berri and Marjan.

The engineering scope includes:

- Production Deck Manifolds (PDMs)
- Installation of approximately 39 km of pipelines
- Subsea facilities and associated infrastructure
- Approximately 41 km of electrical power cables

Why is this interesting?

Offshore oil production is not simply about drilling wells beneath the sea. It requires an integrated network of pipelines, production equipment, electrical systems and subsea infrastructure to move hydrocarbons safely and reliably.

As a Petroleum & Gas Engineering student, I find projects like this valuable because they show how different engineering disciplines come together to make offshore production possible.

Let's discuss: If you were part of an offshore engineering team, which would interest you most: subsea engineering, pipeline installation or production facilities?
